source: Chen et al. (2024/2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models keep producing new solution rounds after the first correct one. Later rounds add almost no accuracy. This is overstaying in a patch whose yield has run out. Self-training on the first-correct solution cut tokens with accuracy kept.
numbers: o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models for 2+3. One example made 13 solutions. The first round was correct in more than 92% of the cases that were correct at all (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1; ASDIV, MATH500) and took under 60% of tokens; QwQ on ASDIV first round 287 tokens = 38.7% of response. Headline: tokens cut 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ with accuracy kept; SimPO alone cut 22.3% on MATH500.
quote: occur more frequently with simple problems
limits: Training-based fix, not a scaffold rule. Easy items dominate the first-correct analysis. The paper defines outcome and process efficiency; neither is a yield-below-average trigger.
agent_relevance: Strong support that the stopping problem exists in reasoning models (gap 10). The fix (stop at first correct) is a sufficiency stop, not an average-rate trigger.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free early exit. At transition words such as 'Wait' the model is asked for a trial answer; if the mean token probability of that answer passes a threshold, reasoning stops. This is a confidence (sufficiency) stop, tested against full reasoning.
numbers: 10 benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC, GPQA, AIME, LiveCodeBench), 11 reasoning models: chain length cut 19.1% to 80.1% on average, accuracy up 0.3% to 5.0%. Confidence is the mean of the max token probability, calibrated with median absolute deviation over several samples.
limits: Read from abstract plus method text of the PDF; per-model tables were not checked line by line. No comparison against a yield-below-average rule or a fixed-step rule inside the paper.
agent_relevance: Best current working example of a probe-then-stop loop. The trial-answer probe costs extra tokens; the paper handles this with a masked KV cache. Gap 2: cheap enough to run inside a budget, at least in this design.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Models usually settle on their final answer after about 60% of the reasoning steps. Stopping when probe answers agree over a window of steps (answer consistency) saves tokens. A repeated answer is a cheap yield measure: no change in the probed answer means zero yield.
numbers: Final answer reached after about 60% of steps on math tasks. Five benchmarks, five open models. Answer Consistency cut tokens by more than 40% on NaturalQuestions while accuracy rose; Learn-to-Stop (supervised on hidden states) cut up to 48% of tokens on NQ with QwQ-32B.
limits: Savings are large on easy and factual sets and smaller on hard sets. The window length k is a tuned parameter; the token curve flattens beyond some k.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: change in the probed answer between steps is a cheap yield measure. Gap 1: it is a trailing-window rule, close to 'recent yield below average' with the average set to zero.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning models know when they're right: probing hidden states for self-verification
finding: A linear probe on hidden states at each intermediate answer predicts whether that answer is correct, with good calibration. Exiting when probe confidence passes a threshold beats a fixed-step exit at equal token cost. This is the closest test of an adaptive stop against a fixed-step stop.
numbers: R1-Distill-Llama-8B on MATH, 10K token cap. Threshold 0.85: accuracy 88.2% (same as no early exit) with about 24% fewer tokens. Threshold 0.9: 88.6% accuracy, 19% fewer tokens. At similar tokens, confidence exit 87.4% (Thr 0.8) versus static exit after m chunks about 82.5%: up to 5 points better. Probe ECE below 0.1; AUC above 0.9 for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME.
limits: One model and one dataset for the exit test. Needs a trained probe and open weights. The adaptive rule is a level (is the answer already right?), not a rate (is the yield falling below average?).
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: adaptive beats fixed-step at equal tokens, by up to 5 points. Still no test of the yield-below-average form. Gap 2: probe score is cheap (one forward pass already done) but not available to a closed-model scaffold.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: The opposite error exists. On hard problems, o1-like models leave a reasoning thought too early and jump to another. Frequent switching goes with wrong answers. This is leaving a patch before it pays.
numbers: Incorrect responses used 225% more tokens than correct ones, with 418% more thought-switching. Two open o1-like models, three hard test sets (MATH500 levels, GPQA, AIME 2024).
limits: Switch count is correlational. The underthinking metric measures the share of tokens in incorrect responses that came after the first useful thought.
agent_relevance: Boundary on any leave rule: a rule tuned to stop overthinking on easy items could worsen underthinking on hard items. Gap 4: hard items sit in an under-stay regime for these models.

source: Wang et al. (2025) same paper: decoding penalty on thought switches (TIP)
finding: Penalising tokens that start a new thought (Wait, Alternatively) makes the model stay longer on each line of thought and raises accuracy without training. This is a direct manipulation of how readily the model leaves.
numbers: On AIME2024 for DeepSeek-R1 the count of thought-switching tokens fell from 13.8 to 5.7 and the mean gap between switches rose from 580.1 to 941.6 tokens. Accuracy gains appear across test sets; a larger penalty helps up to a point, then the benefit plateaus.
limits: Accuracy tables read only in part (garbled extraction); exact accuracy gains not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a higher cost of switching lengthens stays and helps on hard items, as the marginal value theorem predicts for travel time. A tunable stay-bias knob exists.

source: Su et al. (2025) Between underthinking and overthinking: reasoning length and correctness in LLMs
finding: Reasoning models overthink easy questions and fail to lengthen reasoning on hard ones. Length does not track difficulty well, so stay time is not set by patch richness.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill 1.5B and R1-Preview on GSM8K and MATH. Accuracy peaks at a short or medium length rank, not the longest (peak at rank 1 on MATH, rank 3 on GSM8K among length-ranked samples). On questions both models find hard, mean length was not clearly longer than on questions only one finds hard (Table 3, mixed significance).
limits: Small models, two math sets. Preference tuning for shorter responses kept accuracy 'acceptable' but the numbers were not recorded.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10: the stopping problem has two sides. A scaffold needs a signal of difficulty (yield trend), not just a length cap.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does thinking more always help? Mirage of test-time scaling in reasoning models
finding: Forcing more thinking with 'Wait' first raises and then lowers accuracy. Extra thinking raises output entropy, which looks like gain at first. Splitting the same budget into parallel runs with a majority vote does better. This is a measured depletion curve with a peak, and a 'leave and restart' option that wins.
numbers: Accuracy rose from 82.2% to 87.3% as mean thinking tokens went 385 to 1,100, then fell to 70.3% at 15,980. Entropy rose 12x (0.23 to 2.79) when GSM8K thinking went from 385 to 6,136 tokens. Parallel thinking gave up to 20-22% higher accuracy at a 16K budget. Three R1-Distill models; GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2024.
limits: Distilled small models. Forced continuation is not natural stopping.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 3, 4: the yield curve has a peak, so the optimal leave point is real and finite. Leaving the chain (restart or resample) beats staying, which is the MVT shape with travel cost equal to a fresh sample.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Appending 'Wait' (budget forcing) extends thinking and gives gains that flatten. Suppressing the end token too many times pushes the model into repetitive loops. Yield per extra step falls toward zero.
numbers: AIME24 50% to 57% with budget forcing. Scaling flattens at about six times forced continuation. Strings table: 2x 'Wait' 53.3 on AIME24 vs 50.0 for 2x with no string.
limits: One model (s1-32B). The gain per forced step is a diminishing yield, but the paper does not frame it as a leave rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: shows the diminishing curve from which an average-rate threshold could be computed; no one has done so.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (share of problems solved by at least one sample) grows log-linearly with the number of samples and fits an exponentiated power law. Each extra sample adds less. Without a verifier, voting and reward models plateau after several hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples (DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct), above the single-sample state of the art of 43%.
limits: Needs automatic verification to turn coverage into accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 3: a clean yield curve for the 'start a fresh attempt' operator. Marginal gain per sample can be estimated cheaply when the verifier is cheap.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: evaluating and optimizing LLMs for in-context exploration
finding: Handing the model summary statistics or UCB-style numbers in the prompt helps larger models, but they still fall far short of UCB itself. Small models gain little or lose. The model does not fully use a number it is given.
numbers: Overall win rate, multi-armed bandit: raw history Gemini-1.5 Pro 45.5, summarised history 60.0, algorithm-guided support 59.6, UCB 90.6. Flash: 27.7, 34.8, 32.2. Gemma-2B: 7.6, 10.5, 4.9; Gemma-9B: 10.5, 5.3, 4.1. Contextual bandit Pro: raw 7.1, algorithm-guided 64.3, LinUCB 96.4. 30 trials per configuration, t-test p<0.05.
limits: Bandits, not patch leaving. Models are Gemini-1.5 and Gemma-2; no frontier reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: an external statistic helps but is partly ignored. Test the agent with and without the number, and expect a gap to the same rule applied by code.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026, v4) Should you use your LLM to explore or exploit?
finding: Summary statistics fix simple bandits but do not exist for contextual ones. Reasoning models exploit best but are slow and costly. Tool use and in-context summarisation lift medium tasks, yet every LLM tested did worse than plain linear regression.
numbers: Models: GPT-5.2, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen. LLMs help explore large action spaces with meaning by proposing candidates.
limits: Read abstract and introduction only; no result tables recorded. Bandits, not depleting patches.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: compute the yield statistic in code (tool use) rather than asking the model to estimate it. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Zylberberg (2024) Should I stay or should I go? Generalized marginal value theorem with temporal discounting
finding: With exponential discounting and a patch whose rate only falls, the best stay is longer than the undiscounted MVT stay (over-staying). If the rate can rise later, the best stay is shorter (under-staying). An optimal agent can stray either way from the plain average-rate rule.
numbers: Optimal bout duration rises with the discount rate in the monotonic-depletion case (Fig 2C). For the plotted discount rate 1e-6 the shift is small (axis about 6.0 to 6.8); no sample sizes since it is theory. Cites Wispinski for RL agents overstaying more at larger discounting and never under-staying.
limits: Pure theory, preprint, one patch type. No LLM data.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: yes, the best threshold is slightly more patient when yield only falls, but more impatient if later payoffs can jump (insight-style problems). The margin depends on the discount rate; no LLM calibration exists.

source: Wispinski et al. (2023, TMLR) Adaptive patch foraging in deep RL agents
finding: Recurrent RL agents lengthen their stay when patches are further apart, as MVT says. Longer travel time (higher leave cost) gives longer stays.
numbers: Trained 12e7 steps; patch distance 5-12 m in training, evaluated at 6, 8, 10, 12 m with 50 episodes each. Mean leaving step 121.7; mean travel 57.7 steps. Scores higher when patches were closer (p<0.05). Agents overstay plain MVT; discounted MVT fits.
limits: Simulated agents, not LLMs. Re-opened for the travel-time result only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: in agents that learn, switching cost does lengthen stays. A scaffold test would raise the cost of restart (lost context) and measure stay length.

source: Barkett, Long and Kroger (2025) Getting out of the Big-Muddy: escalation of commitment in LLMs
finding: Alone, LLMs did not escalate to a failing investment: they cut the failing division ('rational divestment'). Under peer deliberation or identity ties they escalated strongly. Overstaying in LLMs depends on social framing, not only on yield.
numbers: About 6,500 trials in four studies; advisory study N=2,000. Peer deliberation: escalation 99.2% (249 of 251) versus hierarchical 46.2% (115 of 249). Identity-linked: 97.45% over-allocated; mean allocation 68.95% (SD 9.46%) to the failing division.
limits: Business investment vignettes; model names not captured in the text I checked. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 9, indirect: no search-aversion test. In single-agent mode LLMs lean toward leaving; in multi-agent mode they stay. Do not assume the human bias against switching carries over.

source: Cognitive-bias benchmark (2024) Cognitive biases in LLMs incl. sunk cost
finding: GPT-4o, Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1 were tested on nine biases. GPT-4o and Gemma 2 mostly recognised the irrationality of sunk costs; Llama 3.1 gave contradictory reasoning.
numbers: Nine biases, three models. The text gives 82% for one model in sunk-cost cases; which model was not fixed in my read.
limits: Multiple-choice vignettes. Not a foraging task.
agent_relevance: Gap 9, indirect: LLMs often say the rational thing about sunk costs when asked. A bias may show in behaviour even when it does not in answers; untested.

source: Lacosse, Duarte, Todd, McNamee (2026) Emerging human-like strategies for semantic memory foraging in LLMs (scope re-check)
finding: Re-checked the scope of the fluency study. Only Llama-3 instruct models were used, only animal names, 699 human and 699 generated sequences. No frontier chat model and no other task.
numbers: Switch ratio 0.55 human vs 0.4 LLM (as in the earlier record).
limits: Gap 8 therefore has no support beyond small open models.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: a frontier-model replication on animals plus a non-animal category task is still to run.

source: Search log of this gap pass (arXiv, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, dblp rate-limited; web search worked for one query)
finding: Found no paper that tests a leave-when-yield-below-average rule on an LLM, none that gives an LLM agent per-operator yield memory, and none that measures a bias against searching in LLM agents. One web search for MVT plus LLM returned only RL-agent papers (2210.08085, 2512.12548, Zylberberg 2024).
numbers: Zero direct tests found in this pass. Most search routes returned 429 or budget errors.
limits: Absence is weak evidence. The earlier gap note rested on listing pages; this pass adds one web search and Crossref results (only unrelated hits).
agent_relevance: Keep K15 at single-source. Treat gaps 1, 7, 9 as open for experiment, not for literature.
